questions.text: According to the passage, calculated affection
options: turns into permanent affection over a period of time
appears to be false and fabricated
questions.explanation: The passage says calculated affection is not genuine and is not felt to be genuine by its recipient. That matches the idea that it appears false or fabricated. The other choices are not stated in the passage.

questions.text: Who, according to the passage, is the happy man?
options: One who is free from worldly passions
One who has free affection and wide interests
One who has externally centred passions
One who is encased in self
questions.explanation: The opening sentence defines the happy person as someone with free affections and wide interests. Option B closely restates that definition; the other choices contradict the passage.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true in the context of the passage?
options: The happy man has wide interests.
A man who suffers from the sense of sin must tell himself that he has no reason to feel sinful.
Courage has been recognized as an important virtue.
The issue of intellectual courage has been extensively studied.
questions.explanation: The passage says moral and intellectual courage have been much less studied. Therefore, the claim that intellectual courage has been extensively studied is the statement that is not true.

questions.text: Which of the following virtues, according to the passage, has been recognized for long as an important virtue?
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says courage has been recognized from time immemorial as an important virtue.

questions.text: Which of the following words is similar in meaning to the word 'bestowed' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: “Bestowed” means given or conferred. In the passage, affection is bestowed on the person who gives affection.

questions.text: It is challenging to reply at the spur of the moment when questioned in an interview.
questions.explanation: “At the spur of the moment” means immediately or without prior preparation. “Without delay” is the closest alternative.

questions.text: Rahul was at his wit's end to find that his sister has failed.
questions.explanation: “At one's wit's end” means being so puzzled or distressed that one does not know what to do. “Perplexed” is the closest meaning.

questions.text: He has recovered from illness and now he is as fit as a fiddle.
options: Looks fit but not fit actually
questions.explanation: “As fit as a fiddle” is an idiom meaning healthy and in good physical condition.

questions.text: All three brothers are at loggerheads because of land dispute.
questions.explanation: “At loggerheads” means in strong disagreement or conflict. The land dispute explains why the brothers are in conflict.

questions.text: I am at a loss regarding what to do.
questions.explanation: “At a loss” means uncertain or unable to decide what to do.

questions.text: A man who rarely speaks the truth
questions.explanation: A person who rarely speaks the truth is a liar. “Crook” and “scoundrel” describe wrongdoing more broadly; “hypocrite” means someone whose actions contradict their stated beliefs.

questions.text: The custom of having many wives
questions.explanation: Polygamy is the practice or custom of having more than one spouse. Bigamy specifically concerns having two spouses at the same time.

questions.text: A doctor who treats skin diseases
questions.explanation: A dermatologist is a medical specialist who diagnoses and treats diseases of the skin.

questions.text: A person who studies stars, planets and other heavenly bodies
questions.explanation: An astronomer scientifically studies celestial objects such as stars, planets and other heavenly bodies. Astrology is a different, non-scientific practice.

questions.text: A person who is killed because of their religious or other beliefs
questions.explanation: A martyr is a person who is killed or suffers death for religious beliefs, principles or a cause.

questions.text: Glory — choose the opposite in meaning.
questions.explanation: Glory means great honour or renown. Debasement means degradation or loss of dignity, making it the opposite among the choices.

questions.text: Superiority — choose the opposite in meaning.
questions.explanation: Inferiority is the direct opposite of superiority; it denotes a lower status, quality or position.

questions.text: Testify — choose the opposite in meaning.
questions.explanation: To testify is to give evidence or bear witness. “Falsify” is the closest opposing action among the options because it means to make a statement or evidence false.

questions.text: Repulsive — choose the opposite in meaning.
questions.explanation: Repulsive means causing strong dislike or disgust. Alluring means attractive or tempting, which is the opposite.

questions.text: Expand — choose the opposite in meaning.
questions.explanation: To expand is to make larger or more extensive. To condense is to make more compact or reduce in extent.

questions.text: Cancel — choose the word most similar in meaning.
questions.explanation: To cancel an arrangement or decision is to abolish or annul it. “Abolish” is the closest synonym provided.

questions.text: Germinate — choose the word most similar in meaning.
questions.explanation: To germinate is to begin to grow or sprout, especially when a seed starts developing.

questions.text: Paltry — choose the word most similar in meaning.
questions.explanation: Paltry means very small, meagre or insignificant. “Insignificant” is the closest synonym.

questions.text: Stupid — choose the word most similar in meaning.
questions.explanation: “Dull” can mean lacking intelligence or quick understanding, matching the intended sense of “stupid” in this vocabulary question.

questions.text: Showy — choose the word most similar in meaning.
questions.explanation: Showy describes something conspicuously decorative or ostentatious. “Gaudy” means excessively bright or showy.

questions.text: The man exclaimed that his wallet was stolen.
options: “My wallet was stolen!” the man said.
“Somebody stole my wallet!” exclaimed the man.
The man exclaimed, “My wallet was stolen!”
The man cried, “My wallet was stolen.”
questions.explanation: The reported exclamation changes back to the speaker's first-person pronoun: “his wallet” becomes “my wallet.” Option C preserves the reporting clause and the exclamatory force.

questions.text: Rima said to Priya, “Why are you sketching on the wall?”
options: Rima asked Priya why was she sketching on the wall.
Rima asked Priya why had she been sketching on the wall.
Rima asked Priya that why she is sketching on the wall.
Rima asked Priya why is she sketching on the wall.
questions.explanation: No listed option gives the correct reported question. The grammatically correct form is “Rima asked Priya why she was sketching on the wall”; option A and D incorrectly retain question word order, while B changes the tense/aspect and C is ungrammatical. This item is defective as printed.

questions.text: “Stand at ease,” the soldier said to his men.
options: The soldier told his men that they should stand at ease.
The soldier said to his men that they should stand at ease.
The soldier urged his men to stand at ease.
The soldier commanded his men to stand at ease.
questions.explanation: “Stand at ease” is an order given to the soldiers. “Commanded his men to stand at ease” correctly reports that command.

questions.text: Mr. Swer asked the lady if she could tell him where the nearest post office is.
options: “Where is the nearest post office?” Mr. Swer asked the lady.
Mr. Swer asked the lady, “Could you tell me where the nearest post office is?”
Mr. Swer asked the lady, “Where is the nearest post office?”
Mr. Swer said to the lady, “Where is the nearest post office?”
questions.explanation: Option B restores the polite direct question that corresponds to “asked the lady if she could tell him.” It preserves the embedded question wording and the request form.

questions.text: The Professor said that nobody could solve the problem.
options: The Professor said, “Nobody can solve the problem.”
The Professor said, “Nobody could solve the problem.”
The Professor exclaimed, “Nobody could solve the problem.”
The Professor exclaimed, “Nobody can solve the problem.”
questions.explanation: In indirect speech, “can” commonly backshifts to “could.” Reversing that change gives the direct statement “Nobody can solve the problem.” The original reporting verb is “said,” not “exclaimed.”

questions.text: He suggested that we should be bound by a code of conduct, isn't it? Choose the correct replacement for the underlined part.
questions.explanation: The tag refers to “we should be bound,” so it must use the same modal “should” with a negative form: “shouldn't we?”

questions.text: In order to write poetry, one has to be both sensitive and creative. Choose the correct replacement for the underlined word.
questions.explanation: The sentence is grammatically correct. “Both sensitive and creative” is a valid correlative construction, so no replacement is needed.

questions.text: Bees produce sweet honey as its sting is deadly. Choose the correct replacement for the underlined word.
questions.explanation: The clauses contrast: bees make sweet honey, but their sting is deadly. “But” expresses that contrast; “as” incorrectly suggests a reason.

questions.text: I am tired as I am working since 7 o'clock in the morning.
questions.explanation: The action began at seven o'clock and continues to the present. The present perfect continuous “have been working” is required with “since.”

questions.text: Sheela told her teacher to explain the chapter once again.
questions.explanation: The sentence “Sheela told her teacher to explain the chapter once again” is grammatically valid: “tell someone to do something” is a standard construction. Option C (“asked”) may be more polite pragmatically, but the source provides no context requiring a request rather than an instruction. No unique grammatical error can be established.

questions.text: Rearrange the parts: (a) children / (b) the / (c) were / (d) the animals / (e) fascinated by.
questions.explanation: The parts form “The children were fascinated by the animals”: (b) the, (a) children, (c) were, (e) fascinated by, (d) the animals. The sequence is B-A-C-E-D.

questions.text: Rearrange the parts: (a) plays an / (b) upbringing / (c) important / (d) personal progress / (e) role in.
questions.explanation: The complete sentence is “Upbringing plays an important role in personal progress.” The order is B-A-C-E-D.

questions.text: Rearrange the parts: (a) an / (b) him popular / (c) made / (d) unexpected / (e) victory.
questions.explanation: The parts form “An unexpected victory made him popular.” The sequence is A-D-E-C-B.

questions.text: Rearrange the parts: (a) the coastline / (b) the rugged / (c) they / (d) beauty of / (e) admired.
questions.explanation: The complete sentence is “They admired the beauty of the rugged coastline.” The sequence is C-E-D-B-A.

questions.text: Rearrange the parts: (a) free time / (b) with / (c) little / (d) left / (e) her job.
questions.explanation: The complete sentence is “Her job left her with little free time.” The sequence is E-D-B-C-A.

questions.text: Cloze passage: If you ____ be free from all physical aches and pains and enjoy perfect physical harmony, then put your mind in order and harmonize your thoughts.
questions.explanation: “Can be free” expresses the possibility of being free from physical aches and pains. It is the natural modal construction in this conditional sentence.

questions.text: Cloze passage: put your mind in ____ and harmonize your thoughts.
questions.explanation: The established expression is “put your mind in order,” meaning organise or settle your thoughts.

questions.text: Cloze passage: Let the elixir of goodwill ____ through your veins.
questions.explanation: The idiom is “let something course through your veins,” meaning allow it to flow through the body. “Course” is the correct verb.

questions.text: Cloze passage: ____ your jealousies, suspicions, your worries, your hatreds, your selfish indulgences.
questions.explanation: “Put away” means put aside or get rid of. It fits the instruction to abandon jealousies, suspicions, worries and hatred.

questions.text: Cloze passage: Do not complain when your body is ____ with sickness.
questions.explanation: Both “laid low with sickness” and “laid up with sickness” are established expressions, with slightly different nuances. The sentence supplies no context that reliably excludes either A or D; no unique answer is defensible.

questions.text: Professionals ____ as doctors and lawyers are part of the programme.
questions.explanation: Both “such as” and “like” can introduce examples (“professionals such as/like doctors and lawyers”). The formal register favours “such as,” but the sentence does not make option B grammatically impossible. Flagged as non-unique.

questions.text: The bus stand is directly ____ the police station.
questions.explanation: “Directly behind the police station” is a natural locative construction. “Nearby” is an adverb and cannot directly take the noun phrase “the police station” in this structure.

questions.text: The dogs ____ the field are chasing one another playfully.
questions.explanation: Both “in the field” and “on the field” can be grammatical depending on whether the dogs are described as being within the field or on its playing surface. The sentence provides no further context to distinguish A from C.

questions.text: In accordance ____ the regulations, one must apply for the scheme.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is “in accordance with,” meaning in agreement with or as required by the regulations.

questions.text: The house in ____ I was born has a beautiful garden surrounding it.
questions.explanation: “In which” is the correct relative construction referring to the house as the place where the speaker was born.

questions.text: The speaker's ____ remarks left the audience in awe; his words were both profound and enlightening.
questions.explanation: “Pithy” means concise but full of meaning. That fits remarks described as profound and enlightening; “mundane,” “banal” and “insipid” are negative alternatives.

questions.text: The novel's plot was so ____ that readers were hooked from the first page, unable to predict the twists in the plot.
questions.explanation: “Engrossing” means absorbing or highly interesting, which explains why readers were hooked and could not predictably put the novel down.

questions.text: While her sister was ____ and thrifty, Maria was notoriously extravagant, spending money without a second thought.
questions.explanation: “Frugal” means careful and economical in spending. It contrasts directly with Maria's extravagant spending.

questions.text: The government will ____ the new policy next week, aiming to improve transparency across departments.
questions.explanation: To “adopt” a policy is to formally accept or put it into use. “Adapt” means modify something to suit a purpose.

questions.text: The officer's ____ response to the confrontational question demonstrated her skill in handling complex and sensitive situations.
questions.explanation: “Tempered” can describe a measured, restrained or moderated response. It fits the officer's controlled handling of a sensitive question.

questions.text: Her remarks were intended to be pacifying, but they were interpreted as ____ by the opposition.
questions.explanation: Pacifying remarks are intended to calm people. “Provocative” means likely to anger or stimulate a reaction, so it is the opposite intended here.

questions.text: Unlike the ____ forest they had left behind, the desert landscape was desiccated and bereft of life.
questions.explanation: “Verdant” means green with vegetation. It contrasts with the dry, lifeless desert described in the second part of the sentence.

questions.text: She ____ her mother's stubbornness, always refusing to back down once she's made up her mind.
questions.explanation: “Takes after” means resembles a family member in character or appearance. The sentence says she has inherited her mother's stubborn disposition.

questions.text: The research team had to ____ their procedure after Superintendent pointed out several errors in their experimental design.
questions.explanation: To revise a procedure is to review and amend it in response to identified errors. That is what the team needs to do.

questions.text: The negotiations reached a complete ____, with neither side willing to compromise on their fundamental demands.
questions.explanation: An “impasse” is a deadlock in which progress is impossible because neither side will compromise.

questions.text: The prisoner was released on ____ for good behaviour.
questions.explanation: Parole is conditional release from prison, commonly granted after a period of imprisonment and subject to good behaviour and conditions.

questions.text: Life is to death as pleasure is to
questions.explanation: The relationship is one of opposites: life contrasts with death, just as pleasure contrasts with suffering.

questions.text: Please do not ____ an offer made by the Chairman.
questions.explanation: To refuse an offer is to decline it. “Refrain” requires a different construction, while “refute” means disprove.

questions.text: The police ____ the mob.
questions.explanation: To disperse a mob is to scatter or break up the crowd. The other options do not convey that action.

questions.text: Robert was ____ with a natural talent for music.
questions.explanation: The standard expression is “endowed with a natural talent,” meaning naturally gifted with an ability.

questions.text: If you drink too much, it will ____ your judgement.
questions.explanation: To impair one's judgement is to weaken or damage the ability to make sound decisions. “Impair” is the correct verb.

questions.text: It is very ____ to miss one's train by half a minute.
questions.explanation: Both “annoying” and “exasperating” can naturally describe missing a train by half a minute. “Exasperating” is more emphatic, but the source sentence provides no criterion that makes it uniquely correct.

questions.text: Did you use a dictionary ____ the letter?
questions.explanation: The infinitive “to translate” expresses the purpose for which the dictionary was used.

questions.text: Your case is so unique that I am not getting any ____ to support it.
questions.explanation: A precedent is an earlier case or example that can support an argument or decision in a later case.

questions.text: We thought that the Sadhu had miraculous powers but we soon found out that we were ____.
questions.explanation: To be deceived is to be misled into believing something false. That matches the discovery that the Sadhu did not have the supposed miraculous powers.

questions.text: A temporary departure from the main subject in speech or writing is known as
questions.explanation: A digression is a temporary departure from the main subject in speech or writing. The printed option D is correctly spelled “digression”; option B is printed as the misspelling “digreesion.”

questions.text: Something deserving of ____ praise or admiration is called
questions.explanation: “Laudable” means deserving praise or commendation. It is the correctly spelled word that fits the definition.

questions.text: ____ means unselfish concern for the welfare of others.
questions.explanation: Altruism means unselfish concern for the welfare of others.

questions.text: Maria always wears ____ clothes.
questions.explanation: “Decent clothes” means respectable or suitable clothing. The other options are different words with different meanings.

questions.text: We should always be ____ of what is going on around the world.
questions.explanation: To be conscious of something is to be aware of it. “Conscious” is the correct adjective in this sentence.
